title: Korean Fried Chicken
subtitle: double-fried chicken with sweet-spicy glaze
excerpt: Korean fried chicken is double-fried for an exceptionally crisp coating. The first fry cooks the chicken through. The second fry, at a higher temperature, makes the crust shatter-crisp. It is then tossed in a sweet, spicy, sticky glaze.
sourceNotes: Korean fried chicken (chimaek) exploded in popularity in South Korea in the 1990s and 2000s. The double-frying technique produces a lighter, crispier coating than Western fried chicken. It is traditionally served with beer (chimaek is a portmanteau of chicken and maekju, the Korean word for beer) and pickled radish.

content.text: The double-fry is the technique that sets Korean fried chicken apart. The first fry at a lower temperature cooks the meat through. The second fry at a much higher temperature drives off moisture from the crust so it becomes light and shatteringly crisp. A thermometer makes this much easier to get right.

items.prepNote: bone-in or boneless, cut into pieces
use gochujang Korean chilli paste mixed with a little vinegar -- for the glaze

content.text: Mix the flour, baking powder, and salt in a bowl. Toss the chicken pieces to coat evenly. Shake off any excess.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan to 160C. Fry the chicken in batches for 8 to 10 minutes until cooked through but only lightly coloured. Drain on kitchen paper.
Increase the oil temperature to 190C. Fry the chicken again in batches for 2 to 3 minutes until deep golden and very crisp. Drain on kitchen paper.
Make the glaze: combine honey, soy sauce, gochujang (or chilli flakes with a little vinegar), garlic, and ginger in a small saucepan. Bring to a simmer and cook for 2 minutes until slightly thick.
Toss the hot chicken in the glaze. Serve immediately -- the coating loses its crunch if it sits in the sauce too long.

items.symptom: Coating is soft and not crispy after the second fry
items.cause: Oil not hot enough for the second fry, or chicken not drained properly
items.fix: The second fry must be at 190C. Use a thermometer. Drain the chicken on a rack rather than kitchen paper between fries -- a rack lets air circulate underneath and prevents steam building up.

content.text: Korean fried chicken is a national obsession in South Korea. Thousands of chimaek (chicken and beer) restaurants operate across the country. The double-frying technique is the secret to the famously crisp crust. The glaze can be sweet-soy (ganjang), spicy-sweet (yangnyeom), or plain salted. All are excellent.
